<explanation>
This project is a Linux GPU control application written in Rust, designed to manage and fine‐tune GPU parameters (overclocking, fan control, power and thermal management) for AMD, Nvidia, and Intel GPUs on Linux. The overall design follows a modular, client–server (or daemon) architecture with multiple Rust crates and components that serve distinct roles. Below are detailed guidelines on how to depict an accurate and useful system design diagram tailored for this project:

1. Main Components:
   • Daemon (lact-daemon): Acts as the central service that runs as a systemd service (and/or via OpenRC) and directly interacts with the Linux system interfaces (SysFS, libdrm, kernel drivers) for GPU configuration. It reads a configuration file (e.g. /etc/lact/config.yaml) and listens on a Unix socket and optionally a TCP port.
   • GUI Client (lact-gui): Provides the graphical user interface (using GTK4 and optionally libadwaita) to allow users to view GPU stats, adjust overclocking settings, control fan curves, etc.
   • CLI Utility (lact & lact-cli): Offers a command-line interface to query or change settings, often for scripting or remote access.
   • Client Library (lact-client): Abstracts the communication layer between clients (GUI/CLI) and the daemon by encapsulating the details of exchanging messages.
   • Shared Schema (lact-schema): Contains common API definitions, types (request/response formats), and serialization logic used by both the daemon and client libraries to maintain consistency.
   • Packaging/Deployment Module (pkg directory): Contains build scripts (Makefile), Dockerfiles, Fedora spec files, and packaging recipes—highlighting that the application is designed to be distributed across various Linux distributions.

2. Relationships and Interactions:
   • The GUI and CLI components are clients that communicate with the daemon via the client library (lact-client) using the protocol defined in the shared schema (lact-schema). Arrows should go from the GUI and CLI to the daemon, indicating API calls over Unix/TCP sockets.
   • The daemon itself performs hardware interactions using system libraries (libdrm, hwdata) by reading SysFS and issuing commands to enable/control features. This direct link with underlying Linux system interfaces is a critical design aspect.
   • The packaging components (scripts, spec files, Dockerfiles) are used to build and distribute the application and can be represented as a separate module that “feeds into” all of these deployed artifacts.

3. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Modularization: Notice how the project is separated into multiple Cargo workspaces/crates (each with its own Cargo.toml) corresponding to different roles (daemon, GUI, CLI, client library, schema). The diagram should clearly represent these modules as distinct but interrelated components.
   • Client–Server Architecture: The daemon provides services via an API (both Unix domain socket and optional TCP), and the GUI/CLI operate as separate clients. Indicate directional information flow (e.g., request/response arrows).
   • Separation of Concerns: The user interface (lact-gui) is completely decoupled from the GPU control logic that resides in the daemon. Likewise, the lact-schema and lact-client encapsulate the communication protocol, reducing tight coupling.
   • Extensibility: The file structure and modular design make it evident that new features (or support for additional GPUs) may be added by extending the existing libraries or client modules.

4. Relevant Technologies and Frameworks:
   • Rust programming language with Cargo for dependency management.
   • GTK4 (and libadwaita in lact-gui) for the graphical interface.
   • Systemd for service management (as referenced by the usage instructions in the README).
   • Linux system interfaces (SysFS, libdrm, kernel drivers) for GPU control.
   • Dockerfiles and packaging recipes for multi-distro support.

5. Guidelines for Tailoring Your Diagram:
   • Since this is a full-stack (system-level) application targeting GPU management on Linux, emphasize the clear separation between the front-end (GUI/CLI) and back-end service (daemon). 
   • Clearly distinguish between “control” components (daemon, integration with GPU drivers) and “user” components (GUI and CLI clients).
   • Identify the shared libraries (lact-client and lact-schema) as the bridges that enable communication.
   • Optionally, include the packaging and build layer as part of the deployment pipeline to indicate how the system is distributed.

6. Suggested Diagram Elements:
   • Use distinct colored boxes or shapes to represent each major component:
     - A blue box for the Daemon (lact-daemon).
     - Green boxes for the Client applications (lact-gui and lact-cli/lact).
     - A shared component (such as a grey box with a “common” label) for lact-client and lact-schema.
     - A separate box/area for Packaging/Deployment tools that produce artifacts (pkg directory).
   • Draw directional arrows:
     - From the GUI and CLI boxes to the Client Library box.
     - From the Client Library to the Daemon, indicating API communication.
     - Optionally, annotate these arrows to show “Unix Socket / TCP API calls” or “Request/Response.”
   • Label any external interactions:
     - The daemon’s communications with the underlying Linux kernel and system libraries.
     - The integration with systemd for service management (and configuration file locations such as /etc/lact/config.yaml).

7. Final Diagram Considerations:
   • Be very detailed—include every essential component. Do not merely create a “big box” labeled “lact app” but break it down into the daemon, GUI, CLI, client library, and schema.
   • Ensure that each component is clearly labeled and relationships are evident. Use annotations if necessary to describe configuration details (e.g., “Reads from /etc/lact/config.yaml”).
   • Include legends, color-coding, and directional arrows to reflect how data and control flow through the system.

By following these guidelines, you will produce a comprehensive system design diagram that accurately reflects the architecture of the LACT project. This diagram will help any principal software engineer grasp the modular structure, critical communication flows, and key technologies that underlie the application.
</explanation>
